query: For steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to corrosion? Specify a controlled study capable of revealing the governing cause, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting evidence from prior findings, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In steels designed for high-temperature chemical and nuclear applications, deliberate alloying with aluminum promotes the formation of a continuous, dense Al2O3 surface film that acts as a barrier to oxygen ingress and the dissolution of base metals, thereby enhancing corrosion resistance through the sluggish diffusion of oxygen in aggressive environments.
generation.material_initial_state: Steels such as ferritic/martensitic (e.g., T91) and oxide dispersion strengthened (ODS) steels with comparable base alloying (Cr-rich) but differing Al content prior to corrosion exposure.
generation.intervention: Compare steels with low versus high aluminum content by controlling the aluminum addition in alloy fabrication (e.g., conventional Cr-based versus Cr-Al oxide dispersion strengthened steels).
generation.conditions: Exposure in a high-temperature corrosive environment, such as liquid lead or lead-bismuth eutectic, with a controlled oxygen concentration to simulate service conditions in nuclear reactors or chemical processing equipment.
generation.structural_mediator: An in-situ formed, dense, and continuous Al2O3 oxide layer on the surface of the steel.
generation.mechanism: Due to its high oxygen affinity and favorable thermodynamics, aluminum oxidizes preferentially even at moderate oxygen levels in the liquid metal environment. The resulting Al2O3 film is stable and less permeable, slowing oxygen diffusion into the steel and minimizing the dissolution of alloying elements; this barrier effect, driven by sluggish diffusion through the dense Al2O3 layer, significantly reduces the rate of corrosion.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under identical exposure conditions, steels with higher aluminum content will exhibit noticeably thinner oxide layers, reduced corrosion depths, and improved long-term integrity compared to steels with little or no Al addition.
generation.baseline: Steels without or with lower aluminum content that form primarily less-protective Fe- and Cr-rich oxide films under the same corrosive conditions.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold in high-temperature liquid metal or similarly aggressive corrosive environments with controlled oxygen content; the effect in lower temperature or non-liquid metal environments is uncertain.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal aluminum concentration for maximizing oxidation protection without compromising other material properties is not fully established, and the synergistic effects of other alloying elements (like Cr and Si) may alter the oxide film’s formation and stability.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of steel samples with identical base compositions except for their aluminum content (high-Al vs. low-Al). Expose both sets to a controlled liquid lead environment at 600–700 °C under a fixed oxygen concentration for up to 2000 hours. Post-exposure, analyze the surface and cross-sectional oxide layers using SEM, EDS, and XRD to determine oxide thickness, composition, and continuity, and measure the corrosion penetration depth.
measurements: Oxide layer continuity and phase identification (via XRD and EDS)
Oxygen diffusion rates (if possible, via tracer techniques)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the high-Al samples do not show a statistically significant formation of a continuous, protective Al2O3 layer and reduced corrosion penetration depth compared to the low-Al control group, then the hypothesis that Al-driven oxide film formation is the key mechanism of corrosion resistance is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Traditional steels will be severely corroded in a lead and/or LBE environment, especially when the temperature is higher than 500 °C. The high dissolution rate of the main elements of steel in liquid lead brings great hidden dangers to the safe service of the structure materials. One of the main approaches to fight lead corrosion is to form a protective layer on the surface of the materials by a reasonable control of the oxygen content in liquid lead []. For traditional steel, such as T91, Fe- and Cr-rich oxide layers will form during oxidation, but their structure is not dense enough to protect the matrix, especially at a high temperature. Forming a more stable and protective oxide layer on the surface of steel by optimizing the alloy design received more attention on the materials R&D of LFR in recent years. Al has a strong oxygen affinity; the standard Gibbs formation energy and required oxygen concentration of Al oxidation in lead is lower than those of the Fe, Cr, and Si elements, while the thermodynamic stability of the oxidation product Al2O3 is stronger. The corrosion behavior of T91, 9Cr ODS, and 9CrAl ODS in liquid Pb was tested and compared after exposure up to 2000 h at 600 °C. The main conclusions obtained are as follows: The surface color and luster of the different corrode materials were quite different. The color of T91 is abundant with a metallic luster due to the formation of complex oxidation products and attached lead. Most of the surface of 9Cr ODS is gray-white with a metallic luster due to the covered metallic lead. The color of the 9CrAl surface is quite uniform without metallic luster; The corrosion of 9Cr ODS is slightly heavier than that of T91 after corrosion for 1000 h. An oxide layer that grows outward is locally formed outside of T91, which plays a certain positive role in corrosion resistance, while the fine-grained structure of ODS steel promotes the accelerated dissolution of Fe and Cr, resulting in a lower rate of formation of oxidation products; The maximum corrosion depth of 9CrAl ODS is 51.8 μm after corrosion for 2000 h, which is much lower than that of 9Cr-ODS steel.
